claim: In a 2016 experiment with 10 Japanese participants reading horizontally scrolling Japanese words, reading performance was highest at character sizes of 0.6 to 1.0 degrees of visual angle (tested 0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 3.0), for both 5- and 10-character scroll windows.
quote: reading performance was highest in the range of 0.6° to 1.0°, irrespective of the scroll window size.
title: Effects of Word Width and Word Length on Optimal Character Size for Reading of Horizontally Scrolling Japanese Words

claim: A 2017 Japanese eye-movement study found that breaking lines only between bunsetsu (never splitting a bunsetsu) gave faster reading than the conventional layout at line lengths of 5 to 40 characters per line.
quote: to the conventional text layout with line lengths of 5–40 characters per line. The improvements in reading speed were likely due to the optimization of eye movements near the edge of a line.
title: Readability of Japanese Electronic Text with Bunsetsu-based Layouts
publisher: Transactions of the Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence (J-STAGE)

claim: A Google online experiment (undated page, probably around 2016) reports that three visually redesigned variants of one error message improved both comprehension and resolution over the original message.
quote: we found that the visual variants led to substantial improvements over the original error message in both error comprehension and resolution.
title: The Impact of “Cosmetic Changes” on the Usability of Error Messages

claim: In Inal's 2016 eye-tracking study of web-form error messages (32 participants per another summary), messages placed far from the erroneous field drew fewer saccades and fixations than messages placed near it.
quote: have less saccades to and fixations on error messages compared to those located near to this field
title: User-Friendly Locations of Error Messages in Web Forms: An Eye Tracking Study

claim: In the same 2016 error-message location study, group mean differences were not statistically significant for form completion time, error recognition time, saccade count or error correction time.
quote: were not statistically significant for form completion time, error recognition time, the number of saccades, and error correction time.
title: User-Friendly Locations of Error Messages in Web Forms: An Eye Tracking Study
